newsitem.title: FINLAND: Russia pulls no punches in pre-summit row on NATO.
newsitem.headline: Russia pulls no punches in pre-summit row on NATO.

text.p: Russia, pulling no punches on the eve of a summit with the United States, said on Wednesday NATO expansion would be the West's biggest blunder since the end of the Cold War.

Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky brought to a climax a fierce anti-NATO tirade by Moscow in the run-up to the Helsinki summit which has lowered expectations of a major breakthrough but still left the door to progress open.

"President (Boris) Yeltsin and the Russian leadership are convinced that NATO's plans to expand to the east, if realised, could be the West's biggest strategic mistake since the end of the Cold War," he told reporters.
"It is worth thinking again and again; are there really any concrete reasons -- we are sure there are not -- which demand extending the borders of the bloc eastwards?"
Yastrzhembsky's diatribe set a hostile tone for Yeltsin's summit with U.S. President Bill Clinton on Thursday and Friday, even though it was balanced by some more conciliatory remarks.

He said the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation's plans to offer membership to some former Soviet bloc countries threatened Russia's security and could upset relations with the West less than a decade after the fall of the Berlin Wall.

"I think, much as I would like to be wrong, that we have been robbed to a certain extent of the most valuable achievement of the period since the Cold War -- trust," Yastrzhembsy said in a detailed pre-summit briefing.

"That trust which was built up with such great trouble over many summits between the leaderships of Russia and the United States, and with the leadership of leading Western countries -- it seems to me that trust has been shaken."
NATO's expansion plans are expected to dominate a summit which will also touch on arms control and economic issues and which both sides have said will be tough.

Yeltsin, asserting his authority in the Kremlin again after months of illness, wants to be seen to defend Russia's interests at the summit and has won applause for his tough stance on NATO even from some of his communist and nationalist foes.
It remains unclear how far Russia is prepared to go to to risk a new freeze in relations with the West over an issue which Washington has said it is not prepared to back down on.
Yeltsin said before Moscow's rhetoric toughened late last week that he expected Clinton to show a readiness to compromise and Yastrzhembsky held out hope of measured progress.

"As you know, some summits in the past ended in major decisions, and brought big results and documents. I think this is a bit of a different summit...We would rather expect gradual progress and movement towards mutual strategic goals," he said.

"The reaching of any formal binding document is not foreseen. If there are any agreements we will be very happy. If there are productive, open talks which bring our positions closer, that will also be a good result."

Yastrzhembsky said Russia hoped eventually for a legally-binding agreement with NATO setting out their relations and sought pledges that the Western defence alliance would not move nuclear weapons into the territory of any new members.
NATO is expected to offer membership to some countries from eastern Europe at a summit in July. Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary are thought to be first in line.

Yastrzhembsky ended the day where he had begun, briefing reporters at a specially set-up Russian media centre and mixing optimism with pessimism. He stole a march on the U.S. delegation which held no briefings in Helsinki on the eve of the summit.
